title: Judgment and the Survey Decision
prework: Watch the Module 1 videos, including the short geometric-model bridge. Read the Module 1 note and bring a public company decision for Discussion 1.
output: A draft comparison of detection and construction, a specified benchmark, and one testable prediction for your company decision.

slides.title: Judgment and the Survey Decision
lines: Quantum Cognition for Human-AI Decision Teaming
Nathan Yang
M1S1
slides.notes: This meeting assumes that students have watched the module videos. Use the session for application and assessment progress.

slides.title: Question Order in a Published Survey
lines: What changed before the country question?
slides.notes: Pew reports 78% dissatisfied when the country question came first and 88% when presidential approval immediately preceded it. These are published percentages of U.S. adults, not a new estimate. The page does not supply arm sizes here, so no confidence interval is inferred. Ask students to explain the stable-answer assumption and then name a possible contextual process. The pattern alone does not identify a quantum mechanism. Carry one assumption into Discussion 1.

chart.caption: Pew Research Center, December 2008 U.S. poll.

slides.title: The Same Destination, Different Experiences
lines: Which experience comes first may affect the later choice.
slides.notes: The two illustrated paths reach the same pavilion after encountering a market and a garden in different orders. Treat this as an analogy for sequence, not evidence about human behavior. Translate it into two survey procedures.

slides.title: A Fictional Service Launch
lines: A company must choose how to introduce a data-enabled service.
One survey leads with convenience; another leads with privacy.
The focal outcome is support for launch.
slides.notes: This is a fictional planning case with no reported results. Hold facts fixed. Ask what the manager wants to decide and which customer outcome would be useful. Define data-enabled service in the discussion as a service that uses customer information to provide a benefit.

slides.title: A Fair Comparison in the Survey Tool
lines: The order of A and B varies. F stays last.
Which setting preserves the final decision?
slides.notes: The screenshot is a documented product example, not this course survey. Have students draft the same convenience question A and privacy question B for both ABF and BAF. The launch-support question F stays last. Hold facts, response options, and respondent population fixed. Advanced randomization can preserve positions; do not assume randomizing every question implements ABF versus BAF. Explain how order will be assigned and recorded. Save the wording for the proposal.

image.alt: Official Qualtrics dialog shows no randomization, all-question randomization, a subset option, and advanced randomization. The advanced option is highlighted in the source.

slides.caption: Qualtrics documentation: question randomization.

slides.title: A Fixed-Rate Benchmark
lines: Two assessed action rates are 0.30 and 0.70.
Can any weighted average reach 0.80?
State the assumption that this comparison tests.
slides.notes: Use the displayed line or the Module 3 notebook mixture helper. The values are imposed illustrations, not survey findings. A weighted average cannot exceed both fixed inputs. Applying this benchmark to another procedure requires carrying the conditional rates across procedures. Consider how a process-dependent alternative could change them.

chart.caption: Imposed conditional rates: 0.30 and 0.70; weights range from 0 to 1.

slides.title: A Test of the Alternative
lines: Could attention, memory, or learning explain the difference?
What does that explanation predict?
Which new comparison would distinguish it?
slides.notes: Each group names one specific alternative and an observable implication. A classical process can depend on context. Avoid using classical as a synonym for an unchanging answer. Connect the discussion to the strongest-rival requirement in Project Part 1.

slides.title: Predictions for a New Procedure
lines: Which new observation would separate the models?
slides.notes: The first two values are imposed earlier results that both models reproduce. The final values are competing predictions, not observations. A new procedure is held out when its results are kept separate during fitting and model selection. Ask students to name assumptions that justify their predictions, then write one comparison for their own proposal. These anonymous models illustrate prediction; neither is designated quantum or classical.

chart.caption: Imposed predictions. Both models match the earlier results.

slides.title: The Discussion Argument
lines: Name the company decision and public evidence.
Explain the response procedure and its hidden assumption.
Propose one informative comparison.
slides.notes: Draft an outline for M1A1 using your own company. Peer discussion can improve the reasoning; submit your own post and response under the assessment instructions. Use the public evidence to ground the frames rather than treating the fictional service case as a documented company.

slides.title: The Next Workshop Step
lines: Retain the draft argument and question wording.
Identify one source or design issue to resolve.
Bring the decision statement to Project Studio 1.
slides.notes: Exit note: identify the benchmark, its assumption, and your next evidence-gathering step. This is workshop progress, not a new graded submission.

title: Company Selection and Problem Framing
prework: Bring two public sources about a company decision, your Discussion 1 notes, and the Project Part 1 brief.
output: A feasible company decision, a research question, two candidate frames, and a first entry in the AI Attribution Log.

slides.title: Company Selection and Problem Framing
lines: Quantum Cognition for Human-AI Decision Teaming
Nathan Yang
M1S2
slides.notes: This meeting assumes that students have watched the module videos. Use the session for application and assessment progress.

slides.title: Inputs to a Recommendation
lines: A parent may play music for a child.
Should every play shape future recommendations?
slides.notes: Spotify introduced playlist exclusion in February 2023. Use the displayed nursery-rhyme example to distinguish an observed play from the listener’s preference for future recommendations. The product feature is documented; its effect on satisfaction is a hypothesis to test. Ask students to name a product owner, feasible actions, and an outcome for their own company. Avoid claiming that this interface demonstrates quantum cognition.

image.alt: Spotify’s official nursery-rhyme playlist menu includes Exclude from your taste profile. The source highlights that control.

slides.caption: Spotify launch example, February 2023.

slides.title: Evidence and the Proposed Test
lines: Which claim in your proposal still needs evidence?
slides.notes: The first two entries follow from Spotify’s public example. The audit entry describes a proposed study, not an observed company result. Students add two public sources for their chosen company, recording source, date, and exact supported claim. Keep a company announcement distinct from evidence of causal effectiveness.
slides.caption: Worked source ledger for the Spotify example.

slides.title: Two Competing Considerations
lines: Explain why both considerations matter here.
Write a neutral question for each.
Keep the focal decision separate.
slides.notes: Work on A, B, and F. Ask whether each consideration follows from the institutional setting. Define unfamiliar terms in the question itself. Avoid telling a synthetic respondent how the experiment is expected to turn out.

slides.title: A Research Question You Can Answer
lines: Name the response procedure.
Name the focal outcome and comparison.
State the scope of the model-panel evidence.
slides.notes: A usable question might ask whether the tested model gives different launch-support rates after two specified frame orders. Separate that question from whether real customers support launch. Draft the proposal research question.

slides.title: Volume for a Complete Audit
lines: What volume can you collect and document?
slides.notes: A record here is one completed condition for one persona and repetition. Required records equal personas × six conditions × repetitions. This is accounting, not a precision guarantee, and records need not equal API calls or token costs. Check access, time, approved spending, and the number of calls within each conversation. A pilot tests the workflow. Use the collection guide and record the scope feedback before project collection.

chart.caption: Six conditions per persona. Counts exclude retries and pilot work.

slides.title: Peer Review of the Proposal
lines: Can a reader identify the management decision?
Do the frames follow from the public evidence?
Is the strongest alternative specific and testable?
slides.notes: Exchange draft outlines. Give one substantive suggestion tied to a proposal rubric criterion. Each student decides how to revise their individual work.

slides.title: Your Judgment and AI Use
lines: Write your reasoning before using AI assistance.
Log the tool, prompt, and resulting changes.
Explain what you accepted, revised, or rejected.
slides.notes: Project Part 1 is AIAS 3. Follow the assessment instructions and keep the AI Attribution Log. The log should document judgment, not merely list a tool name.

slides.title: The Proposal Draft
lines: Save the decision, sources, and three draft questions.
Record the scope feedback.
List the remaining design choices for Module 2.
slides.notes: This checkpoint prepares the proposal due at the end of Week 2. Consult Canvas for the exact date. It is not an additional graded deliverable.

title: Interpreting Order Effects
prework: Watch the Module 2 videos, including intervals and tolerances. Run the order-and-QQ notebook and bring a preliminary A/B/F battery.
output: A correct QQ interpretation, a defined focal order comparison, and draft thresholds and rival tests for the proposal.

slides.title: Interpreting Order Effects
lines: Quantum Cognition for Human-AI Decision Teaming
Nathan Yang
M2S1
slides.notes: This meeting assumes that students have watched the module videos. Use the session for application and assessment progress.

slides.title: Order Differences and QQ
lines: Which statistic compares F across orders?
Which statistic compares A/B agreement?
What records does each require?
slides.notes: Give students two minutes to write their answers. The focal difference uses F yes rates; q uses actual paired A/B responses within each order. Clarify only the distinctions that remain uncertain.

slides.title: An Imposed Answer-Pair Table
lines: Both columns contain 100 illustrative interviews.
slides.notes: The table consistently uses A rows and B columns, including for BA. These are imposed counts and not human observations. Students should verify totals before computing rates.

slides.title: Agreement and the A-Yes Rate
lines: Why can agreement stay fixed while an answer rate changes?
slides.notes: A-yes is (30+10)/100=.40 in AB and (45+25)/100=.70 in BA. Agreement is (30+40)/100=.70 in AB and (45+25)/100=.70 in BA, so q=.00 for the agreement-difference definition. A-yes is a marginal answer rate, not F. This table contains no F responses; it cannot establish a focal decision effect. Ask students which records their proposal needs for each statistic.

chart.yTitle: Share of 100 interviews in each order
chart.caption: Calculated from the imposed answer-pair table on the previous slide.

slides.title: A Classical Sequential Explanation
lines: Inspect the transition rules in the notebook.
The rules vary with which question comes first.
Which extra prediction would test this explanation?
slides.notes: Run classical_order_example. In AB, A yes is .4 and B yes conditional on A is .75 or 1/3. In BA, B yes is .5 and A yes conditional on B is .9 or .5. Ordinary probabilities generate the table with q=0. Source: the course’s constructed example; Dzhafarov and Kon, https://arxiv.org/abs/1710.07847.

slides.title: Intervals Against a Practical Range
lines: Use a prespecified tolerance of ±5 percentage points.
slides.notes: The intervals are illustrative inputs, not estimates from a dataset. Ask students to classify each and justify the action. A and C lie inside the practical range; B is unresolved. Revise the table if the class chooses a different managerial tolerance.

slides.title: Resampling Complete Personas
lines: Which six records travel together when a persona is drawn?
slides.notes: Each of three personas has one record in each of six conditions. One bootstrap draw selects persona 02 twice, persona 03 once, and persona 01 zero times. Copy all six records each time a persona is selected. This example explains the resampling unit; three personas are not an adequate sample-size recommendation. For the course audit, retain the complete persona blocks and all repetitions in each selected block. For independently assigned human respondents, the resampling design would follow the actual human sampling structure.

chart.caption: Toy example: draw personas 02, 02, 03 from three complete blocks.

slides.title: Design Revisions
lines: Freeze A, B, F, coding, and collection conditions.
Choose a practical threshold and q tolerance.
Write a fair test of the strongest alternative.
slides.notes: Students revise their own proposal. Thresholds should follow the managerial decision and feasible precision. The teaching value of .05 is not a universal threshold. Save the rationale in the proposal and log any later changes.

slides.title: The Interpretation Paragraph
lines: Explain why order and QQ answer different questions.
Describe what an uncertain interval leaves unresolved.
Use that reasoning in Discussion 2.
slides.notes: Write a short outline for M2A1 and identify one remaining proposal weakness. Submit individual work under the brief. Next session is the battery-design workshop.

title: Battery Design and Proposal Workshop
prework: Bring the draft proposal, question battery, evidence ledger, and collection guide. Review the Part 1 rubric.
output: A revised proposal with fixed wording, six conditions, a persona plan, thresholds, and explicit actions for different findings.

slides.title: Battery Design and Proposal Workshop
lines: Quantum Cognition for Human-AI Decision Teaming
Nathan Yang
M2S2
slides.notes: This meeting assumes that students have watched the module videos. Use the session for application and assessment progress.

slides.title: A Battery for the Service Decision
lines: How would you revise these questions for your company?
slides.notes: A battery is a set of questions used together. These shortened prompts illustrate structure; students must specify the service, features, privacy practices, and neutral wording. In the constructed ABF and BAF arms, keep F last and retain actual prior answers. Follow the collection guide for all six conditions. Define any specialized terms in the survey itself.
slides.caption: Fictional planning example. Supply the same service facts in every arm.

slides.title: Six Conditions, One Persona Grid
slides.notes: The isolated conditions ask every question in a fresh conversation. Constructed conditions retain actual prior answers. Direct and assessed arms supply the separate procedural comparison. An ordinary all-at-once panel is optional and does not replace a required arm.
table: A, B, F / B, A, F
A → B → F / B → A → F

slides.title: The Final Question Has a Fixed Position
lines: Randomizing questions and selecting a subset change different things.
Which items vary, and which position stays fixed?
slides.notes: Use this product example to inspect a design choice before collecting data. The screenshot shows a general control, not a configured ABF/BAF study. Students identify how their implementation preserves F last while varying A and B. Hold the fact sheet, coding, and intended context fixed. Pilot both orders and save the exact prompts, actual answers, and conversation history.

image.alt: The upper portion of the official advanced-randomization dialog contrasts fixed display order with randomize questions. The displayed example text belongs to Qualtrics, not the course battery.

slides.caption: Qualtrics documentation: advanced randomization.

slides.title: The Record of What Each Person Saw
lines: The assigned order and the observed order should agree.
Can your records reconstruct the question sequence?
slides.notes: Qualtrics documents an option to export viewing order. The course model-panel workflow needs the analogous evidence: condition, persona, repetition, actual prompt order, response, and conversation history. Set the collection volume, model version, settings, and stopping rule before collection. Students save a pilot record and verify it can reproduce a response path. This slide does not require students to use Qualtrics.

image.alt: An official Qualtrics export dialog has the option Export viewing order data for randomized surveys checked and outlined.

slides.caption: Qualtrics documentation: viewing-order export.

slides.title: Precision and the Collection Plan
lines: How does this uncertainty compare with your practical threshold?
slides.notes: The displayed normal-approximation half-width for a difference is 1.96 × sqrt(0.25/n+0.25/n) ×100 percentage points, where n is observations per independent arm. Values are about 19.6, 13.9, 9.8, 6.9, and 4.9 points. This conservative planning illustration is not the audit’s paired-persona bootstrap interval or a sample-size prescription. Dependence, rare subgroups, and invalid answers affect precision. Students freeze their substantive thresholds and appropriate analysis before observing the project results.

chart.xTitle: Observations per arm (each step doubles n)
chart.caption: Planning illustration: two independent arms, each with yes probability 0.50.

slides.title: Peer Review Against the Rubric
lines: Find one claim without enough evidence.
Find one design choice that could change the result.
Propose a concrete revision.
slides.notes: Partners use the M2A2 rubric and collection checklist. Keep feedback specific. Each student owns the final proposal and discloses permitted AI assistance.

slides.title: Revisions and Their Reasons
lines: Resolve the highest-impact issue first.
Record what changed and why.
Preserve the original prediction for comparison later.
slides.notes: Allow quiet revision time. A useful revision log separates planned design changes from changes made after results are observed. The log later supports Project Part 2 and the reflection.

slides.title: Proposal Submission Check
lines: Attach the proposal, battery, sources, and AI log.
Check the exact Canvas deadline.
Retain a fixed copy before collecting project data.
slides.notes: Use M2A2 for the complete requirements. This workshop does not add a separate submission.

title: Handoffs, Recommendations, and Evidence
prework: Watch the Module 3 videos. Read the Meridian and Juno examples in the Module 3 note. Complete the short interference notebook.
output: A draft Discussion 3 comparison, an interpretation of the direct-versus-assessed evidence, and a proposed managerial outcome for the report.

slides.title: Handoffs, Recommendations, and Evidence
lines: Quantum Cognition for Human-AI Decision Teaming
Nathan Yang
M3S1
slides.notes: This meeting assumes that students have watched the module videos. Use the session for application and assessment progress.

slides.title: An Interface Suggests the Next Action
lines: An extra identity check changes the payment process.
What does the reviewer see before choosing?
slides.notes: Stripe’s public product page illustrates review suggestions and an option to start an authentication experiment. Adaptive 3DS refers to an additional identity check for a payment. The displayed revenue number is part of a company demonstration, not a measured result for our case. Ask students where a recommendation, risk assessment, or interim answer enters the decision process. Compare a direct decision with a decision after an explicit assessment while holding the underlying facts fixed. Manual review is described at https://docs.stripe.com/radar/transaction-reviews.

image.alt: The focused view of the official Stripe demo displays an Adaptive 3DS recommendation with a Start experiment control. 3DS adds customer authentication. Its revenue number is demo content.

slides.caption: Stripe public interface demonstration, captured November 2026.

slides.title: Meridian’s Illustrative Console Choice
lines: Conditional block rates: 0.63 and 0.41.
Fraud-judgment share: 9/11; assessed rate: 0.59.
Direct block rate: 0.69.
slides.notes: Meridian is fictional and these rates are illustrative. Ask students to calculate the weighted rate and identify what comparison is challenged by .69. Source: Nathan Yang, Case: The Intermediate Step; adapted to distinguish the fixed-rate benchmark from process-dependent alternatives.

chart.caption: Fictional Meridian example; imposed rates, not field estimates.

slides.title: The Meaning of the Difference
lines: Compute direct minus assessed.
State why 0.69 lies outside the fixed-rate bracket.
Name a process that could change conditional rates.
slides.notes: The difference is .10 and the bracket is [.41,.63]. The weighted identity holds within assessed records. Carrying its rates to the direct procedure is the additional assumption. Ask groups to propose an informative comparison rather than assert that every classical explanation has failed.

slides.title: Equal Block Rates, Different Errors
lines: Which outcomes matter beyond the block rate?
slides.notes: Both procedures block 40 of 100 attempts. A blocks 25 fraudulent and 15 legitimate payments; B blocks 10 fraudulent and 30 legitimate payments. Fraud not blocked is therefore 5 versus 20. These are imposed workshop counts with known ground truth, separate from Meridian’s decision rates. A block rate alone does not measure accuracy or welfare. Students specify a managerial outcome and the validation evidence needed for their own setting.

chart.caption: Imposed outcomes: 30 fraudulent and 70 legitimate attempts in each procedure.

slides.title: Listening and the Taste Profile
lines: A play can serve a temporary purpose.
What outcome would show that recommendations improved?
slides.notes: Spotify’s 2025 announcement documents a track-level exclusion control. The pictured distinction gives a real setting for Juno’s recommendation problem from the videos. Ask students to separate immediate playback, future recommendations, and the outcome the listener values. A temporary use does not by itself reveal a stable preference. Propose a comparison and a measure of recommendation quality; do not infer effectiveness or a quantum mechanism from the feature’s existence. Save the comparison for Discussion 3.

image.alt: Spotify’s official track menu shows Hide in this playlist separately from Exclude track from your taste profile. The latter is highlighted in the original image.

slides.caption: Spotify track-exclusion announcement, October 2025.

slides.title: What the Panel Represents
lines: Tier 1 checks the calculation using a simulator.
Tier 2 studies the model under documented prompts.
Tier 3 adds evidence from relevant people.
slides.notes: Have each group rewrite an overbroad sentence into a claim about the observed unit. A synthetic persona is not a human respondent. Bisbee et al., https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2024.5, provide a comparison between synthetic outputs and human survey evidence.

slides.title: The Assessment Draft
lines: Outline the handoff or recommendation issue for M3A1.
Name the outcome your project recommendation needs.
Bring the completed M3A2 run to the studio.
slides.notes: Give students individual writing time. The discussion brief specifies the post and peer response. The practice notebook is an ungraded checkpoint; it prepares the collection and analysis workflow.

title: Audit Workshop and Troubleshooting
prework: Complete M3A2. Bring its executed notebook, your fixed proposal, collection records if available, and the Project Part 2 brief.
output: A checked collection structure, executed analysis or documented blocker, and a draft evidence table for the report.

slides.title: Audit Workshop and Troubleshooting
lines: Quantum Cognition for Human-AI Decision Teaming
Nathan Yang
M3S2
slides.notes: This meeting assumes that students have watched the module videos. Use the session for application and assessment progress.

slides.title: The Practice Result
lines: Did the calculation recover the simulator’s pattern?
How did the smaller sample change the intervals?
Which warning needs attention?
slides.notes: Students compare estimates with known population values in their own run. A small sample can leave a decision unresolved even when the code is correct. Do not alter seeds until a preferred finding appears.

slides.title: A Missing Condition in the Collection
lines: What must be resolved before calculating the paired comparison?
slides.notes: This small record excerpt is a debugging exercise, not a dataset to analyze. Missing is not No. Inspect the full six-condition collection, distinguish failed calls from refusals and parser errors, and follow the frozen inclusion rule. Do not silently drop or impute a record. Preserve raw responses and count denominators explicitly. Students verify their own collection with the supplied audit code.
slides.caption: Toy excerpt: two of the six conditions; one repetition per persona.

slides.title: Estimates Across Repeated Samples
lines: Where does your reported uncertainty come from?
slides.notes: This is a sampling simulation, not a bootstrap of collected data. In each of 5,000 repetitions, independently draw two binomial counts with n=100 and probabilities 0.60 and 0.50, then subtract the rates. NumPy default_rng seed 20261111. Five-point bins are left-closed, right-open except the last. The true difference is 10 percentage points. The audit instead resamples complete observed persona blocks to preserve dependence. Students run their notebook and verify counts, q, the focal difference, and bracket diagnostics against raw records. Simulation source and counts are provided in source/sessions.json.

chart.xTitle: Difference in percentage points (5-point bin midpoints)
chart.caption: 5,000 simulations: 100 independent responses per arm; true rates 0.60 and 0.50.

slides.title: The Rare Subgroup Limits Precision
lines: Which conditional rate will be less precise?
slides.notes: A conditional rate computed from ten records generally has less information than one computed from ninety, holding the response variance and dependence structure comparable. Here both subgroup counts are imposed. Empty groups can make a conditional rate or bracket unavailable. More bootstrap draws do not create additional observations. Students inspect subgroup sizes, invalid records, and the inclusion rules before interpreting an uncertain result.

chart.caption: Imposed counts: 100 assessed records divided by the first answer.

slides.title: Peer Critique of the Evidence
lines: Does each estimate have a clear denominator?
Does the interval preserve the sampling structure?
Does the interpretation stay within Tier 2?
slides.notes: Exchange a summary table without sharing private or unnecessary raw records. Use the Part 2 rubric to identify one claim to narrow or one check to strengthen.

slides.title: The Result Paragraph
lines: State the tested model, procedure, and outcome.
Report magnitude and uncertainty together.
Connect the finding to a proposed action.
slides.notes: Draft the report using actual results or explicitly mark a workflow draft if collection is incomplete. Explain the strongest alternative near the interpretation it limits.

slides.title: Remaining Work
lines: Save the notebook, records, and revised evidence table.
Log any departure from the proposal.
Assign your next analysis or collection step.
slides.notes: The report is individual. Preserve the original design and explain revisions. Consult Canvas and M4A1 for the submission and presentation requirements.

title: Audit Presentations and Oral Defense
prework: Prepare the individual 6–10 slide deck and rehearse a ten-minute presentation. Review M4A1 and the no-AI oral-defense rule.
output: The individual presentation and oral defense, plus recorded feedback for the final report.

slides.title: Audit Presentations and Oral Defense
lines: Quantum Cognition for Human-AI Decision Teaming
Nathan Yang
M4S1
slides.notes: This meeting assumes that students have watched the module videos. Use the session for application and assessment progress.

slides.title: Presentation Block
lines: Ten-minute individual presentation.
Five minutes of questions.
Up to six presenters in a 90-minute block.
slides.notes: Display before presentations. The 90 minutes belong to six 15-minute slots. Briefing instructions should be read before the meeting. If the cohort exceeds six, the instructor schedules additional blocks. The following slides are reference prompts and do not add time.

slides.title: A Figure for the Client Decision
lines: What evidence belongs next to these rates?
slides.notes: This public preparation example uses imposed counts, not a student solution or a real company result. Students should identify the tested model and persona design, define each sequence, report the 13-point difference with an appropriate interval, and show how it affects the decision. The bars alone do not establish statistical precision or human customer behavior. In the client story, connect the decision, design, uncertainty, strongest alternative, and recommendation. This reference slide adds no time to the six 15-minute presentation slots.

chart.yTitle: Support rate in the model panel
chart.caption: Illustrative audit: 128/200 versus 102/200 valid responses.

slides.title: A Recommendation Depends on Costs
lines: At what error cost would your recommendation change?
slides.notes: The horizontal variable c is the cost of one error of the type that occurs 5 times under A and 15 times under B. The fixed losses are 70 and 40 units. A and B tie at c=3 with loss 85. All costs and counts are imposed for oral-defense preparation. A manager must justify both counts and valuations. Students use their own evidence to name a review condition and identify the assumption that supports their broadest claim. The oral defense is AIAS 0.

slides.title: Averages and Subgroup Patterns
lines: Which comparison deserves a question from the reviewer?
slides.notes: Equal group weights yield a pooled rate of .60 in both orders, while subgroup changes run in opposite directions. The four subgroup counts are 80,40,40,80 yes out of 100. This descriptive example does not supply intervals or establish subgroup effects. Ask about prespecification, uncertainty, and the relevance of subgroup definitions. Peer feedback should identify a supported claim and a missing link to the action. Students revise their individual reports using their actual evidence; this slide is a public preparation prompt.

chart.caption: Imposed rates: 100 observations per profile in each order.

slides.title: After the Presentation
lines: Record the feedback that affects your recommendation.
Revise the report and document the change.
Retain the evidence supporting your final judgment.
slides.notes: Use the revision log in the collection guide. The final written submission remains governed by M4A1 and the Canvas deadline.

title: Audit Synthesis and Reflection
prework: Bring your results, presentation feedback, revision log, and reflection brief. Watch the Module 4 videos before the meeting.
output: A revised recommendation, a completed final-submission check, and individual notes for the 800-word reflection.

slides.title: Audit Synthesis and Reflection
lines: Quantum Cognition for Human-AI Decision Teaming
Nathan Yang
M4S2
slides.notes: This meeting assumes that students have watched the module videos. Use the session for application and assessment progress.

slides.title: The Scope of the Evidence
lines: What was the unit of observation?
Which procedure changed?
Which conclusion was best supported?
slides.notes: Students answer from their own audit. Use the three questions to establish comparable descriptions before discussing patterns across projects.

slides.title: Three Audit Summaries
lines: Which comparison is justified across these settings?
slides.notes: Audits 1,2,3 have imposed estimates .5,1,10 and illustrative 95% intervals [-2,3],[-12,14],[6,14]. These are not class results, computed intervals, or a pooled estimate. First compare the model, persona grid, question wording, population, and outcome. Then consider effect size, precision, and each prespecified practical threshold. Replace the demonstration with volunteered class summaries during discussion. Do not interpret the number of positive intervals as a common effect.
slides.caption: Imposed estimates and 95% intervals, in percentage points. Different settings.

slides.title: Costs of Two Review Procedures
lines: How robust is the $100 difference to your assumptions?
slides.notes: These are imposed expected costs for a workshop comparison, not measured returns or a recommendation for Stripe. Fraud losses fall by $600, while customer friction rises by $500. Customer friction means the cost of legitimate users facing extra checks, delay, or rejection. The total saving is $100 per 1,000 decisions. Ask what uncertainty or omitted cost would change the ranking and what a human pilot would need to measure. Compare the actions supported by the actual class audits.

chart.caption: Imposed costs: total $2,800 versus $2,700 per 1,000 decisions.

slides.title: A New Test of the Strongest Alternative
lines: What must stay fixed when you add a delay?
slides.notes: Both proposed explanations reproduce a ten-point immediate order difference. The first predicts decay after a specified delay; the second predicts persistence. These predictions are imposed conditional examples, not universal predictions of classical or quantum theory. A delay may also change memory, attention, or information. Specify its duration, hold other features fixed, and state assumptions that make the comparison informative. Students revisit the rival in their proposal and identify what evidence would change the recommendation.

chart.caption: Imposed rival predictions; no outcomes from the proposed delay test.

slides.title: The Revised Recommendation
lines: Name the action and responsible owner.
State the evidence that supports it.
Add a condition for review.
slides.notes: Individual revision time for Project Part 2. Connect the recommendation to the strongest defensible finding. Keep broader human claims tied to the human evidence that would be needed.

slides.title: Reflection Notes
lines: What did you initially expect?
What evidence changed or confirmed your reasoning?
Which habit will you carry into another decision?
slides.notes: The reflection is AIAS 1. Students write their own reflection; AI may be used only for permitted brainstorming. Use this period for independent notes from the proposal, results, and revision log. The target is 800 words, with details in M4A2.

slides.title: Final Submission Check
lines: Report, executed notebook, records, deck, and logs.
Check that the figures match the reported estimates.
Submit through the Canvas assignment links.
slides.notes: Use the complete M4A1 and M4A2 instructions. Keep source files and private records in the approved location. Exact deadlines and any instructor arrangements are in Canvas.
